plan.title: What your elements do at work
How you burn out, and how you come back
Feedback: taking it and giving it
The job vibe that fits you

intake.question: Where are you with work right now?
What drains you most at work?

options.label: Boredom, the same thing every day

strong.text: Your chart is strong, so this style comes at full intensity. You can work long and hard without external motivation, and you trust your process. The risk is that you set the pace for everyone around you without noticing. Check in with colleagues on timelines rather than assuming they'll keep up. Being fast is a strength; being the only one who knows the plan is a bottleneck.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Share the plan out loud. Speed alone makes you a bottleneck.

weak.text: Your chart is the lighter kind, so this style shows up best when you feel supported. In the right team you're quietly excellent; in a hostile one you second-guess yourself. Choose environments carefully, and keep a record of your wins. Weak charts often forget their successes and remember every mistake, which skews how you see your own work.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Keep a wins file. Your memory only saves the mistakes.

wood.heading: Your email style
wood.text: Wood writes emails that point somewhere. Subject line with a verb, a clear ask, a next step and a date. Colleagues like knowing what you want. The habit to watch is the long 'one more thing' paragraph at the end, where three new projects quietly sneak in. Send those as separate emails, later. One email, one direction, is the Wood rule that keeps people actually reading you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Wood email rule: one email, one direction. Extras go later.

fire.heading: Your email style
fire.text: Fire writes warm emails: exclamation marks, thanks, a friendly line about the weekend. People enjoy hearing from you. The risk is that the actual request gets buried under the warmth, and nobody acts on it. Put the ask in the first two lines, then be as lovely as you like. And never answer an email that made you angry within the hour. Fire types send the reply they regret fastest.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fire email rule: the ask in line one. Angry replies wait an hour.

earth.heading: Your email style
earth.text: Earth writes reliable emails. You reply, you confirm, you follow up when others forget. Your inbox is a small act of care for the whole team. The habit to watch is over-explaining: three paragraphs of context before the point, in case anyone feels left out. Try bullet points and a short summary up top. Steady and short reads as confident, not cold.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Earth email rule: summary on top, bullets below. Short reads confident.

metal.heading: Your email style
metal.text: Metal writes short emails. Sometimes very short. 'Fine.' 'No.' 'See attached.' Efficient, and occasionally terrifying for the person on the other end, who reads it three times looking for anger that isn't there. Add one human line. 'Thanks for the quick turnaround' costs four seconds and saves a colleague a worried afternoon. Precise doesn't have to mean frosty.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal email rule: add one human line. Four seconds, much kinder.

water.heading: Your email style
water.text: Water writes thoughtful emails, sometimes so thoughtful they arrive three days late. You want to answer properly, so you wait until you have time, and then the thread has moved on. Try a quick holding reply: 'Got it, full answer by Thursday.' It keeps the current moving. Your deep replies are worth waiting for; people just need to know they're coming.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Water email rule: a quick 'got it, more by Thursday' keeps things flowing.

wood.heading: Your element at work: Wood
wood.text: Wood at work is growth and direction. Wood people need to feel they're developing, a new skill, a bigger scope, a project that's getting somewhere. Stagnation is the Wood nightmare: the same role for years with nothing to learn. You also tend to plan ahead and think in terms of where you'll be next year. Make sure your manager knows your growth goals, because Wood without a direction grows sideways, into frustration.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Wood needs growth. Tell your manager where you want to grow.

fire.heading: Your element at work: Fire
fire.text: Fire at work is visibility and energy. Fire people do their best work when it's seen and appreciated: presenting, pitching, leading the kickoff, celebrating the launch. You light up teams. Long invisible projects with no recognition dim you quickly. Ask for moments to show your work, and build in rest, because Fire burns brighter than it can sustain.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fire needs an audience. Ask for chances to show your work.

earth.heading: Your element at work: Earth
earth.text: Earth at work is reliability and care. Earth people hold teams together, keep promises and build systems that last. You value stability and get uneasy with constant change. Your work is often underrated because it's steady rather than dramatic. Make your contribution visible, and when change comes, ask for the reasons. Earth adapts well once it understands why.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Earth adapts fine once it knows why. Ask for the reasons.

metal.heading: Your element at work: Metal
metal.text: Metal at work is precision and decisiveness. Metal people cut through noise, set standards and finish things. You like clear rules, clear goals and clear accountability. Vague cultures frustrate you. Your challenge is softness: delivering standards with warmth so people want to meet them rather than fear missing them.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal sets the bar. Deliver it warmly so people want to reach it.

water.heading: Your element at work: Water
water.text: Water at work is intelligence and adaptability. Water people see the big picture, connect ideas and navigate change easily. You need intellectual stimulation and some freedom in how you work. Rigid processes feel like a dam. Your challenge is focus: choosing where your current goes so it carves a canyon instead of spreading into a marsh.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Water needs a channel. Pick where your current goes.

base.how-you-work:
Gap Wood works like a tall pine grows: straight up, toward a goal you can see from far away. You need a clear direction before you can give your best. Hand you a vague brief and you'll spend the first week rewriting it into something with a spine. Once the direction is set, you're relentless. You start early, you finish what you start, and you hate leaving a task half done over a weekend.

You work best on projects that build over time: a product launch, a team you grow from three people to ten, a skill you sharpen for years. Quick wins bore you a little. You like work that will still be standing next year.

Your habit worth watching is taking on too much because you assume you're the only one who'll do it properly. Sometimes you're right. Often someone else would do it at ninety percent, and ninety percent from them frees you for the thing only you can do.

base_panels.speaker: bom
base_panels.text: The tall pine at work: straight up, toward a goal.

base_panels.speaker: yeon
base_panels.text: Give you a fuzzy brief and you hand back a real plan.

base_panels.speaker: bom
base_panels.text: You take the wind first so your team doesn't have to.

spring.intro:
You're Wood born in spring, a young tree in a forest that is all growing at once. Element match: your birth season carries your own element, so at work you start out sure of how you like to operate. You have a strong default style and you settle into a new job fast. The flip side is friction with workplaces that run on a very different rhythm. You'd rather change jobs than change your whole way of working, and sometimes that's exactly right.

For Gap Wood at work, this season shapes how fast you climb and how much shade you give the people under you along the way.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Strong default style. Sometimes the job has to fit you.

summer.intro:
Wood born in summer is a tree in full leaf under a hot sky, green and generous and a little thirsty. You pour into the season: your birth season draws your element outward. At work that makes you a doer and a maker: you need to produce something visible, a project, a design, a result you can point to. Jobs that are all meetings and no output leave you restless. The risk is overproducing and running yourself down, so build in recovery the way you build in deadlines.

For Gap Wood at work, this season shapes how fast you climb and how much shade you give the people under you along the way.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You need to make something visible. Meetings alone won't do it.

earth.intro:
Your Wood arrived in the Earth days that close a season: a tree with its roots wrapped around heavy soil. You shape the season: your element works on the season you were born in. At work that's a results person: you like targets, tangible progress and the satisfaction of managing resources well. You're good at turning messy situations into organized ones. Watch for treating every week like a quarter-end close. Not everything needs optimizing.

For Gap Wood at work, this season shapes how fast you climb and how much shade you give the people under you along the way.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You'd optimize your lunch break. Not everything needs a plan.

autumn.intro:
Picture Wood born in autumn: a tree in the season of the axe, when the air turns sharp and the leaves come down. The season tests you: the season you were born in presses on your element. At work that gave you discipline and a strong sense of responsibility early. You respect structure, meet deadlines and handle authority well. You can also be hard on yourself and slow to ask for help. A boss who praises as well as corrects brings out your best.

For Gap Wood at work, this season shapes how fast you climb and how much shade you give the people under you along the way.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Disciplined since forever. You deserve a boss who praises too.

winter.intro:
Wood born in winter is a bare tree with its roots deep in cold, wet ground, quietly drinking. The season feeds you: your birth season feeds your element. At work that looks like someone who learns quickly and benefits enormously from good mentors, training and support. You absorb a workplace's knowledge like soil absorbs rain. Choose jobs where people will teach you, because you turn teaching into skill faster than most.

For Gap Wood at work, this season shapes how fast you climb and how much shade you give the people under you along the way.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Pick jobs with great teachers. You learn faster than anyone.

base.how-you-work:
Eul Wood works like a vine: you find the path around obstacles that stop everyone else. You're adaptable, socially smart and quietly persistent. Give you a project blocked by politics, budgets and three departments that don't talk to each other, and you'll have it moving within a month, mostly through conversations people barely remember having.

You work best with variety and people. Long solitary tasks drain you. Collaborative projects, client work, anything where relationships move things forward, that's where you shine. You're also good at reading what a boss actually wants versus what they said, and delivering the first.

The habit to watch is overcommitting socially. You say yes to every coffee, every committee, every favor, because each one is a thread in your web. Then your own deep work happens at 11 pm. Guard a few hours a week where no one can reach you.

base_panels.speaker: bom
base_panels.text: The vine at work: you find the path nobody else sees.

base_panels.speaker: yeon
base_panels.text: Three departments that don't talk. You fix it with coffees.

base_panels.speaker: bom
base_panels.text: Your team stays for years because you notice things.

Byeong Fire works like the sun: big energy, wide reach and a habit of lighting up whatever you point at. You're at your best at the start of something, the pitch, the launch, the kickoff where enthusiasm is the fuel. People want to work on your projects because you make them feel exciting.

You think out loud, generate ideas fast and get bored with maintenance. Spreadsheets that need updating every week are your nemesis. You're also generous with credit and quick to celebrate other people's wins, which makes you a magnet for good collaborators.

The habit to watch is the gap between launch and finish. Suns rise beautifully and the afternoon can drag. Pair yourself with a detail person, use deadlines you announce publicly, and celebrate finishing as loudly as you celebrate starting.

Jeong Fire works like a candle: focused, warm and steady, lighting the exact spot that needs it. You're the colleague who notices the detail everyone missed, the tone of the email that will upset the client, the slide that contradicts the data. Your attention is precise and your care is real.

You work best in depth rather than breadth. One meaningful project you can pour yourself into beats ten shallow ones. You're often the emotional intelligence of a team, sensing tension before it surfaces and quietly fixing it. People trust you with sensitive things.

The habit to watch is overgiving. Candles burn themselves to make light. You'll stay late polishing work nobody asked to be polished, and absorb your team's stress as if it were your job. It isn't. Set a finishing line for each task before you start it.

Mu Earth works like a mountain: steady, reliable and very hard to move once you've settled on a plan. You're the colleague everyone trusts with the critical stuff, the year-end close, the client who's about to leave, the system that can't go down. You don't panic. You show up, you do the work, and you keep doing it.

You work best with stability and clear responsibilities. Constant reorganizations and shifting priorities make you grumpy, because you like building something solid and then maintaining it properly. You're patient with long projects and excellent at holding the details of complex operations in your head.

The habit to watch is resistance to change. You can dismiss new ideas because the current way works. Sometimes it does. Ask yourself, when you feel the 'no' coming, whether you're protecting quality or protecting comfort.

Think of Gi Earth as the garden field at work: fertile, practical and quietly productive. You make things grow, projects, people, systems, through steady care rather than dramatic moves. You notice what a project needs before anyone asks, whether that's a timeline, a checklist or a colleague who needs encouragement.

You're organized, adaptable and deeply helpful. You're the one who knows where the files are, who remembers what was decided three meetings ago, and who quietly fixes the gaps between departments. Teams run more smoothly with you in them, often without realizing why.

The habit to watch is invisible labor. You do so much behind the scenes that nobody sees it at review time. Keep a running list of what you fixed, organized and rescued. Share it. Being humble is lovely; being forgotten at promotion time is not.

At work that's a results person: you like targets, tangible progress and the satisfaction of managing resources well. You're good at turning messy situations into organized ones. Watch for treating every week like a quarter-end close. Not everything needs optimizing.

For Gi Earth at work, the season decides what your field grows: other people's projects first, or finally a harvest with your name on it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You'd optimize your lunch break. Not everything needs a plan.

base.how-you-work:
Gyeong Metal is the sword at work: decisive, efficient and allergic to waste. You cut through confusion, make the call when everyone else is hedging, and finish the job. Meetings that could have been emails physically pain you. You like clear goals, clear ownership and the satisfaction of a problem solved cleanly.

You work best under pressure and with real stakes. Crises bring out your best: you get calm, sharp and fast. You're also fiercely loyal to teams that earn your respect and blunt with people who don't.

The habit to watch is cutting too fast. You can kill an idea before it's had a chance to develop, or make a decision before you've heard the quiet person with the crucial detail. Count to five in meetings before you rule on something. The best swords know when to stay in the scabbard.

base_panels.speaker: bom
base_panels.text: The sword at work: you make the call while others hedge.

base_panels.speaker: yeon
base_panels.text: Meetings that could be emails cause you physical pain.

base_panels.speaker: bom
base_panels.text: Emergency? Everyone looks at you. You don't flinch.

base.how-you-work:
Sin Metal brings the jeweler's eye to work: refined, precise and quietly perfectionist. You notice what others miss, the typo on slide 14, the inconsistency in the brand guide, the clause that will cause problems in two years. Your work is polished, and you'd rather deliver late than deliver something you're embarrassed by.

You work best with high standards and clear quality bars. Sloppy environments upset you on a physical level. You're excellent at refining things: taking a rough draft, a messy process or a raw product and making it shine.

The habit to watch is perfectionism as procrastination. Sometimes you don't start because you can't do it perfectly yet. Set a 'good enough for version one' rule and polish in rounds. Jewels are cut in stages, not in one perfect strike.

base.how-you-work:
Im Water at work is the ocean: big-picture, restless and full of ideas. You see connections nobody else sees, between markets, between departments, between a problem in one place and a solution from somewhere completely different. You think in systems and strategy. Routine bores you almost instantly.

You work best with freedom and complexity. Give you a huge, messy problem and some autonomy and you'll come back with a strategy nobody expected. You're also good with change: reorganizations that terrify others feel like weather to you.

The habit to watch is drifting. You can start ten things and finish three, lose interest once the idea is clear, and leave the details to someone who wasn't consulted. Partner with finishers, write down what you've committed to, and treat follow-through as part of the creative work.

base.how-you-work:
Gye Water at work is the rain: gentle, intuitive and everywhere. You soak up information others miss, the mood in a meeting, the unsaid concern of a client, the trend before it's a trend. Your work is thoughtful and often quietly brilliant, and people sometimes underestimate it because you don't announce it.

You work best in calm, supportive environments where you can think. You're adaptable, imaginative and good with research, writing and anything that needs intuition. You're also the team member who notices a colleague is struggling and quietly helps.

The habit to watch is invisibility. You can be so adaptable and low-key that your contributions disappear into the group. Put your name on your ideas. Send the follow-up email that says 'here's what I found.' Rain matters most when people notice it.

base_panels.text: Your team speaks freely because you made it safe.
